Inside Stockholm’s Vasa Museum, visitors stand beside a large, intricately rigged model of a seventeenth-century sailing warship, with cream-colored sails, rows of cannons, and brightly painted red, yellow, and gold ornamentation. Looming behind it is the immense dark wooden hull of the original *Vasa*, a Swedish warship commissioned by King Gustavus Adolphus. The ship sank in Stockholm harbor on its maiden voyage in 1628 and was raised in 1961, remarkably well preserved. The colorful model, built at one-tenth scale, reconstructs how the ship probably appeared when new, before centuries underwater stripped away its brilliant paint.

The sinking was caused by the ship's top-heavy design: a gust of wind tipped it far enough for water to flood through the open lower gunports. It had sailed only about 1.3 kilometers.

An intricate, symmetrical cosmic mandala in deep indigo, ivory, and luminous gold. Four translucent, overlapping petals containing celestial landscapes surround a radiant golden circle with an empty center. Delicate geometric lines, interconnected spheres, and repeating arches extend into a star-filled cosmos, suggesting infinite recursion. On the left, a sword-like beam of light cuts through crystalline formations. Lotus flowers float above reflective waters below. The composition evokes Buddhist emptiness, dependent origination, and the inexhaustible interplay of form and formlessness.
